after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
For what reason does the function $f(x)$ given below have a discontinuity at $x=2?$

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}, & x<2 \\ 4, & x=2 \\ -2x, & x>2\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2.$

- $f(2)=4,$ so $f(2)$ exists. $✓$

- We calculate the one-sided limits and check if they coincide:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}(-{x}^{2}) \\  & =-{2}^{2} \\  & =-4, \\ {lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}(-2x) \\  & =-2\cdot 2 \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the overall limit exists and ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)=-4$ $✓$

- The limit of the function is not equal to the function value: ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)=-4,$ while $f(2)=4.$ $\,\,\times $

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=2$ because ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)\ne f(2).$
